assertion: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
warehouse_value: AZ Apr-Aug 2026 1,938 vs 2025 2,391 thousand MWh (-19%), lowest 2010-2026; AZ-only vs 10-yr mean about -33% (state proxy)
independent_value: EIA: 19% below last year, 28% below 10-yr average, record low
sql: SELECT generation_year, state_abbr, SUM(generation_thousand_mwh) FROM energy.eia_electricity_generation WHERE geo_level='state' AND sector_code='99' AND energy_source_code='HYC' AND state_abbr IN ('AZ','NM','NV') AND generation_month BETWEEN 4 AND 8 GROUP BY generation_year, state_abbr

assertion: At the end of September, Lake Powell's depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
independent_value: EIA: Powell 3,518 ft vs 3,490 ft (0.8%); Mead 1,038 ft vs 950 ft (9.3%)

assertion: Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.
independent_value: EIA STEO Nov 2026 (projection): SW 6.13 BkWh in 2026 (24% below 10-yr avg); 2027 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower

assertion: Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.
reason: No primary plant-level figure found. The only EIA-based reporting read (Land Desk via Coyote Gulch) gives Glen Canyon 2.75 TWh (269,370 homes) and Hoover 'about the same', roughly 5.5 TWh, which would not be nearly seven; EIA's whole Southwest region total in 2025 is about 6.7 BkWh, so the piece may have used the regional figure. Warehouse state totals (AZ 4,783, NV 1,881 thousand MWh in 2025) include other plants and cannot isolate the dams.
measure: hydroelectric net generation monthly by state

assertion: Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River.
independent_value: USGS Circular 1502 as relayed by secondary sources: high mountain terrain (~15% of Upper Basin) yields ~85% of annual flow; other estimates 70-80% (definition-dependent)

sources.title: USGS how much snow for Colorado River flow

searched: Colorado River snowpack provides about 85% of annual flow Rocky Mountains

assertion: Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years.
independent_value: Reclamation/CRS describe continuous drought since 2000 (26-27 years)
searched: Colorado River Basin drought 2000 2026 megadrought Reclamation

assertion: Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low.
independent_value: Reports: Powell up 20-22 feet since mid-September record low, still about 26% full
searched: Lake Powell elevation rise October November 2026 storms flooding

assertion: In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.
independent_value: IEA: +1.1% (410 Mt), hydropower shortfall about 170 Mt (~41%); IEA report page returned 403, confirmed via IEA news page in search
searched: IEA CO2 Emissions in 2023 hydropower shortfall 40%

assertion: Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts.
independent_value: Wasti et al. 2022 WIREs Climate Change review identifies glacier loss, reduced seasonal snow storage, greater variability and higher evaporation as the main pathways (via Columbia Climate School coverage; Wiley page 403)
searched: 2022 review climate change impacts on hydropower WIREs wcc.757
